slides.headline: There's a skull hidden in this painting. Can you see it?
slides.sub: Hans Holbein the Younger, The Ambassadors, 1533

slides.headline: That strange shape on the floor
slides.text: It's a skull, painted stretched out. Look at it from the lower right, almost from the side of the painting, and it snaps into shape.

slides.headline: Why hide it?
slides.text: A reminder of death in a room full of wealth and power. Walking past the painting, you would suddenly see it, as if death appeared out of nowhere.

slides.headline: Top left, half hidden
slides.text: A small crucifix peeks out from behind the green curtain. Easy to miss, and probably meant to be.

slides.headline: Their ages are written in the painting
slides.text: Jean de Dinteville's dagger sheath reads 29. Georges de Selve's book, under his elbow, says 25.

slides.headline: The latest technology
slides.text: The upper shelf holds a celestial globe and instruments for measuring time and the stars. Status symbols for educated men.

slides.headline: A broken string
slides.text: Look closely at the lute: one string has snapped. Often read as a sign of discord in a Europe split by religion.

slides.headline: The hymn book
slides.text: Next to the lute lies an open hymn book with Lutheran hymns, painted in the years when the Reformation was tearing Europe apart.

slides.headline: Even the floor means something
slides.text: The patterned floor is modelled on a famous medieval pavement in Westminster Abbey.
